1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: Male patient, 67-year-old overseas Chinese entrepreneur, chief complaint: "recurrent chest tightness for 1 year, exertional dyspnea for 3 months, worsening for 1 week," was admitted to our hospital for the first time on Day 0. One year earlier, the patient was diagnosed with interstitial lung disease abroad because of "chest tightness after activity" and was given antifibrotic therapy; intermittent home oxygen therapy (2 L/min) improved the chest tightness. Three months earlier, the patient developed exertional dyspnea, accompanied by cough, sputum production, and palpitations, with self-measured oxygen saturation of 80%-90%. After methylprednisolone tablets 20 mg/day were added at a local hospital, symptoms were somewhat relieved and he was able to travel. Two months earlier, when methylprednisolone was gradually tapered to 12 mg/day as instructed, chest tightness and dyspnea worsened again, and he required oxygen from a portable oxygen concentrator (3 L/min) while walking to maintain oxygen saturation. One month earlier, the patient presented to a hospital in China, where testing showed positive antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (perinuclear type), and chest CT suggested bilateral interstitial pneumonia, partial interstitial fibrosis in both lower lungs, and elevated right hemidiaphragm. Further electromyography suggested multiple peripheral nerve injuries, moderate to severe. Diaphragmatic electromyography suggested severe abnormal motor conduction of the right phrenic nerve. It was considered that the current worsening dyspnea was related to right diaphragmatic paralysis, and that the diaphragmatic paralysis might be related to his cervical spondylosis. Gradual tapering and discontinuation of glucocorticoids were recommended, and noninvasive ventilation was given to improve dyspnea symptoms. One week earlier, the patient's dyspnea worsened again, with self-measured oxygen saturation decreasing to 53% after activity, accompanied by chest tightness and palpitations. He came to our emergency department and was subsequently admitted to our department. The patient was obese (body mass index: 32.42 kg/㎡), with a past history of hypertension, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and cervical spondylosis. He denied a history of chronic airway disease and had a history of lumbar disc surgery more than 30 years ago. He denied food or drug allergy history. Smoking history was 100 pack-years. He drank baijiu 20 mL/day with an alcohol history of more than 30 years, and has now quit smoking and alcohol for 1 year. Family history was unremarkable. Physical examination: pulse: 90 beats/min, respiration: 20 breaths/min, blood pressure: 137/81 mmHg, temperature: 37.3℃. Alert, in fair general condition, on nasal oxygen at 3 L/min, SpO2: 96%, no cyanosis of the lips, no palpable enlargement of superficial cervical lymph nodes, no jugular venous distention, decreased breath sounds in the right lung, Velcro rales audible in the left lower lung. Regular heart rhythm, no murmur heard. Abdomen flat and soft, no tenderness or rebound tenderness. Muscle atrophy in both lower extremities, decreased reflexes, high arches, no obvious sensory disturbance. No edema in both lower extremities. Laboratory tests: arterial blood gas analysis: pH 7.43, PaCO2 50.10 mmHg↓, PaO2 56.60 mmHg↑, oxygenation index 171 mmHg. Complete blood count: WBC 8.5×10⁹/L, NE% 56.8%, EOS 0.15×10⁹/L, LY 2.84×10⁹/L, CRP: 3.8 mg/L. Myocardial function testing: creatine kinase-MB: 16 U/L, troponin-T: 0.023 ng/mL. Serum potassium: 2.99 mmol/L↓; liver function, renal function, and BNP were all normal. Urinalysis: urine protein 1+. Coagulation: PT 13.7 s, APTT 34.1 s, FIB 2.53 g/L, D-Dimer <220 ug/L (FEU). Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody: ANCA (perinuclear type) 1:20; ANCA (cytoplasmic type), anti-MPO antibody IgG, and anti-PR-3 antibody IgG were all negative; antinuclear antibody testing: negative; myositis antibody panel: negative; antiphospholipid antibody: negative; rheumatoid factor: <9.3 IU/mL; ferritin: 155.7 ug/L; sialylated carbohydrate antigen (KL-6): 1039.54 U/mL↑; immunoglobulins: IgG: 8.28 g/L↓, with no obvious abnormalities in IgA, IgM, or IgG4. Absolute immune cell count panel: B-cell count (CD19+): 895.17/μL ↑, B cells (CD19+): 30.89% ↑, with no other abnormalities. Ancillary examinations: sinus and chest CT (outside hospital Day -39): 1. Consider bilateral interstitial pneumonia (fibrotic NSIP?), partial interstitial fibrosis in both lower lungs, decreased compared with outside hospital CT on Day -146. 2. Aortic and coronary atherosclerosis, enlargement of the main pulmonary artery. 3. Elevated right hemidiaphragm. 4. Gallstones included in the scan. 5. Bilateral maxillary sinusitis and ethmoid sinusitis. Coronary angiography (outside hospital Day -39): 1. Diffuse mixed plaques in the vessel wall of the proximal to mid left anterior descending artery and segmental mixed plaques in the vessel wall of the obtuse marginal branch, with severe luminal stenosis; scattered mixed plaques throughout the vessel wall of the right coronary artery and localized calcified plaque in the vessel wall of the first diagonal branch, with mild luminal stenosis; localized calcified plaque in the vessel wall of the left main coronary artery and localized calcified plaque in the vessel wall of the proximal left circumflex artery, with slight luminal stenosis. 2. Right coronary dominance. 3. Slightly enlarged left ventricle; left atrial appendage well visualized, with no filling defect seen. 4. Suspected pulmonary hypertension: aortic sclerosis. Pulmonary artery and bronchial artery angiography (outside hospital Day -38): the main pulmonary artery was slightly enlarged, pulmonary hypertension could not be excluded; no embolism was seen in the pulmonary arteries above the subsegmental level; no definite tortuous enlargement of the bilateral bronchial arteries was seen. Echocardiography (our hospital Day +2): left atrial enlargement, left ventricular hypertrophy; decreased left ventricular stroke volume index, accelerated left ventricular outflow tract velocity due to hyperdynamic left ventricular state (under loading conditions); degenerative change of the aortic valve; mitral annular calcification of the posterior leaflet, estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 32 mmHg. EF: 66.4%. High-resolution CT of the lungs (our hospital Day +5): bilateral interstitial lung changes; bilateral emphysema, pulmonary air cysts, pulmonary bullae; chronic bronchitis; scattered fibrous proliferative foci in both lungs; coronary artery and aortic calcification, widened pulmonary artery; elevated right hemidiaphragm.

differential_diagnoses.name: Acute exacerbation or progressive worsening of interstitial lung disease (predominantly in the fibrotic NSIP spectrum)
supporting_evidence: Has a history of interstitial lung disease diagnosed abroad, and has previously received antifibrotic therapy and home oxygen therapy

Chief complaint: recurrent chest tightness for 1 year, exertional shortness of breath for 3 months, worsening for 1 week, with a marked decrease in oxygen saturation to 53% after activity, suggesting recent worsening of underlying pulmonary parenchymal disease.
Chest CT at an outside hospital suggested bilateral interstitial pneumonia (fibrotic NSIP?), with partial interstitial fibrosis in both lower lungs.
Pulmonary HRCT at our hospital showed "interstitial changes in both lungs; scattered fibrotic proliferative foci in both lungs"
On physical examination, Velcro crackles were audible in the left lower lung, consistent with signs of interstitial lung disease
Elevated KL-6 1039.54 U/mL, supporting active interstitial lung injury/alveolar epithelial injury
Arterial blood gas showed hypoxemia (PaO₂ 56.60mmHg, oxygenation index 171mmHg)
The attached CT images show diffuse reticular/interstitial changes in both lungs, more pronounced in the peripheral and lower lungs, with fibrotic changes.
opposing_evidence: Inflammatory markers are not elevated: WBC 8.5×10⁹/L, CRP 3.8 mg/L, not supporting an acute inflammatory process clearly triggered by infection

An outside-hospital CT on Day -39 showed 'partial interstitial fibrosis in both lower lungs, decreased compared with the outside-hospital CT images from Day -146,' indicating that the imaging findings were not unidirectionally and continuously progressive.

differential_diagnoses.name: ANCA-associated disease-related interstitial lung disease (especially ILD associated with the ANCA-associated vasculitis spectrum)
supporting_evidence: Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody was perinuclear pattern positive; an outside hospital had previously found “anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (perinuclear pattern) positive”; this time ANCA (perinuclear pattern) 1:20
Persistent bilateral interstitial pneumonic/fibrotic changes on lung imaging, which may be seen in ANCA-associated disease-related ILD
The patient has moderate-to-severe multiple peripheral nerve damage; peripheral nerve involvement can be seen in systemic vasculitis spectrum disorders.
Urinalysis showed urine protein 1+; although nonspecific, it suggests the need to be alert to the possibility of systemic involvement.

Symptoms were previously relieved after corticosteroid therapy; after dose reduction, chest tightness and shortness of breath worsened again, suggesting the possibility of an immune-inflammatory disease.
opposing_evidence: Anti-MPO IgG antibody and anti-PR3 IgG antibody were both negative, reducing support for typical ANCA-associated vasculitis
ANA negative, myositis antibody panel negative, rheumatoid factor normal, with no other definite evidence of systemic autoimmune disease provided
The phase 1 information did not describe typical manifestations of small-vessel vasculitis such as hemoptysis, epistaxis, purpura, and progressive renal dysfunction.
CRP is not elevated, and peripheral blood eosinophils are not elevated, which does not support significant active systemic inflammation or eosinophilic vasculitis.

differential_diagnoses.name: Hypoventilation due to right diaphragmatic paralysis/phrenic nerve dysfunction, exacerbating dyspnea
supporting_evidence: Diaphragmatic electromyography at an outside hospital indicated "severely abnormal right phrenic nerve motor conduction," and it was explicitly considered that "this exacerbation of dyspnea is related to right diaphragmatic paralysis"
Imaging repeatedly indicated "right diaphragmatic eventration/right hemidiaphragm elevation"
Physical examination showed "decreased breath sounds in the right lung," consistent with elevation of the right hemidiaphragm and restricted ventilation.
Arterial blood gas showed PaCO₂ 50.10 mmHg, suggesting a tendency toward hypoventilation.
The patient is obese (BMI 32.42 kg/㎡), with increased diaphragmatic load, which can make dyspnea due to diaphragmatic dysfunction more pronounced.
Marked shortness of breath after activity, requiring an increased supplemental oxygen flow rate, consistent with exertional dyspnea after decreased ventilatory reserve
opposing_evidence: Imaging also shows definite bilateral interstitial changes and fibroproliferative foci, suggesting that the dyspnea cannot be fully explained by diaphragmatic factors alone
Velcro crackles in the left lower lung and elevated KL-6 are more supportive of coexisting parenchymal lung disease.
The Phase 1 information did not provide more direct evidence supporting the severity of diaphragmatic paralysis, such as supine dyspnea, orthopnea, or postural changes in vital capacity.

differential_diagnoses.name: Emphysema/chronic bronchitis with pulmonary fibrosis (CPFE spectrum or mixed obstructive-restrictive lung disease)
supporting_evidence: A 100 pack-year smoking history is a high-risk factor for emphysema and chronic airway disease
HRCT of the lungs at our hospital showed: "emphysema, pulmonary cysts, and bullae in both lungs; chronic bronchitis; interstitial changes in both lungs"

The attached CT images show areas of increased pulmonary lucency and cystic changes, along with bilateral reticular/fibrotic interstitial changes, consistent with the imaging features of coexisting emphysema and fibrosis.
There is significant hypoxemia, and CPFE may present with relatively severe gas exchange impairment.
Pulmonary artery enlargement; patients with CPFE often have concomitant pulmonary vascular involvement or a tendency toward elevated pulmonary arterial pressure
opposing_evidence: The patient denies a history of chronic airway disease.
The physical examination did not describe obvious wheezing or other typical signs of COPD, such as long-term copious sputum production.
Velcro crackles in the left lower lung and elevated KL-6 more strongly suggest an interstitial lung disease component.

recommended_exams.exam: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, anti-MPO antibody IgG, anti-PR-3 antibody IgG
Brain MRI without contrast + SWI + diffusion-weighted imaging

stage2_input.text: The patient's ECG suggested abnormal Q waves in the inferior leads and ST-T segment changes; coronary CTA at an outside hospital suggested severe luminal stenosis of the proximal-to-mid left anterior descending artery and the obtuse marginal branch. A cardiology consultation was first requested and coronary angiography was completed immediately, which intraoperatively showed 80% stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending artery, 60% stenosis of the second diagonal branch, 60% stenosis of the left main coronary artery, and 30% stenosis of the proximal right coronary artery. During the procedure, two 3.5*38mm stents were implanted in tandem in the left anterior descending artery segment.

exclusion_reasons: Involvement of both lungs is not severe; compared with the CT images from Day -146, there is slight improvement. Oral corticosteroids and antifibrotic therapy are effective, which cannot explain the worsening chest tightness and shortness of breath.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: CMT genetic testing was completed; no pathogenic or likely pathogenic mutations were detected.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has multiple peripheral neuropathies, moderate to severe, muscle atrophy of both lower extremities, decreased reflexes, and pes cavus, and is also accompanied by severely abnormal right phrenic nerve motor conduction and right hemidiaphragm elevation, suggesting that in addition to immune-related nerve involvement, hereditary peripheral neuropathy such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease should also be differentiated. The purpose of this test is to determine whether the chronic peripheral neuropathy and phrenic nerve involvement have a genetic basis, to avoid misclassifying hereditary neuropathy as vasculitis or other secondary lesions; if a pathogenic mutation is detected, it may change the interpretation of multisystem involvement and the subsequent treatment direction; if no pathogenic or likely pathogenic mutation is detected, this helps reduce the likelihood of hereditary peripheral neuropathy as the primary cause, thereby supporting continued integration of the diagnosis from the perspective of ANCA-associated immune disease and selection of immunotherapy.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: CMT genetic testing was completed, and no pathogenic or likely pathogenic mutations were detected; non-contrast brain MRI + SWI + diffusion imaging was completed, with results suggesting a few ischemic lacunar lesions in the bilateral frontoparietal lobes and periventricular regions. Further testing including TB infection T-cell testing, the pre-treatment four-item panel, hepatitis B serologic markers, and HBV-DNA was completed to exclude active infection. The patient's TB infection T-cell test showed MTB antigen (ESAT-6): 12, MTB antigen (CFP-10): 0, suggesting a positive TSPOT.

8.final_diagnosis_and_diagnostic_basis.final_diagnosis: ANCA-associated vasculitis, hypertension, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes mellitus
diagnostic_basis: After 5 days of gamma globulin therapy, the patient subjectively reported some relief of chest tightness and shortness of breath, hypoxemia improved significantly, and SpO2 was 92% without supplemental oxygen; gamma globulin therapy was considered effective.
History of hypertension, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and type 2 diabetes mellitus

treatment_plan: Gamma globulin 20 g/day × 5 days, one course per month, for 6 consecutive months
Rituximab 1000 mg on D1 and D15
Adjunctive sulfamethoxazole for prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
treatment_response: Chest tightness and shortness of breath have improved significantly compared with before, and the patient has now been completely weaned off oxygen.
Repeat chest CT showed that the interstitial changes in both lungs were slightly improved compared with Day +2, and there was no obvious improvement in right hemidiaphragm elevation.
